theme: The tongue; worldliness; humility before God
readingInstruction: Read James 3:1-4:17. Two themes run through these chapters: the power of the tongue and the war between friendship with the world and humility before God. Notice the contrast between wisdom from below and wisdom from above.
settingTheScene: James is writing to churches where speech was causing division. Teachers were quick to claim authority, and quarrels were breaking out among believers. James traces conflict to its source in the heart and calls the church to humble repentance. In Jewish wisdom writing, the tongue and the heart were closely tied, and James follows this tradition, with echoes of Proverbs and the teaching of Jesus.
observation: “How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire!” (3:5).
“No human being can tame the tongue” (3:8).
“But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere” (3:17).
“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you?” (4:1).
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (4:6).
“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (4:8).
“For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (4:14).
“So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (4:17).
interpretation:
James begins with a warning for teachers: “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness. For we all stumble in many ways.” Anyone who does not stumble in what he says is a perfect man. Then come the pictures: a bit in a horse’s mouth, a rudder on a ship, a spark in a forest. The tongue is small but steers the whole body. “So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire!” It is “a world of unrighteousness” and “set on fire by hell.” Every kind of creature has been tamed by mankind, “but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” Our greatest inconsistency is that “with it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.” A spring does not pour out fresh and salt water. Only the Spirit can change the heart so that the mouth follows.

James then contrasts two kinds of wisdom. Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are “earthly, unspiritual, demonic,” and where they are found, there is disorder and every vile practice. “But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” This is a checklist for every conflict.

In chapter 4, James asks where conflict comes from: “What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?” We desire and do not have, so we murder (in heart); we covet and cannot obtain, so we fight. We do not have because we do not ask, or we ask wrongly, to spend it on our passions. He calls his readers “adulterous people,” echoing the prophets’ language of God’s people unfaithful to their covenant husband: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.” But God gives more grace: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

The remedy is a series of commands: “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.” Grieve over sin, and “humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.” Do not speak evil of one another, since it makes you a judge of the law instead of a doer. The chapter closes with a warning to the self-assured planner: “You do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.” Instead, say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” And one summary sin: “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.” Sins of omission count.
connection: Proverbs 18:21 says death and life are in the power of the tongue. Matthew 12:34-37 teaches that the mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance. Ephesians 4:29 and Colossians 4:6 direct our speech. Genesis 1:26-27 is behind the “likeness of God.” Hosea 2 and Jeremiah 3 use adultery as an image of unfaithfulness. Proverbs 3:34 is quoted in 4:6, and 1 Peter 5:5-9 echoes it. Matthew 5:9 blesses peacemakers. Proverbs 27:1 and Luke 12:16-21 warn about boasting about tomorrow. Psalm 39:5 and 90:5-6 describe life as a breath.
application:
Before you speak in a hard conversation today, run it through verse 3:17: is it pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, and merciful?

Name a quarrel and ask what desire is behind it (4:1-2). Confess it to God, and make the first move toward peace.

Practice saying “If the Lord wills” as you plan the week, and mean it.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what your tongue has done.
Ask him to change your heart because you cannot tame your tongue.
Ask him to give you wisdom from above.
